title: On the Inscrutable Judgments of God

blocks.s: Since the second species of contemplation, following Bernard, concerns the judgments of God, something may be said of these most wonderful and inscrutable judgments. Augustine, in the twentieth book of The City of God, chapter two, treats this beautifully: we learn to bear with equanimity the evils that good people suffer, and not to prize the goods that evil people attain; and thus even in those matters where divine justice does not appear, divine teaching is salutary. For we do not know by what judgment of God this good person is poor and that wicked one rich; why the one who ought to be tormented for his dissolute life rejoices, while the one whose laudable life should earn gladness is saddened; why the innocent is crushed in judgment and the wicked justified. All these things, says Augustine, are inscrutable now; but when the day of the final judgment comes, not only what is then judged, but all that has been judged from the beginning and that remains to be judged until that day, shall appear most just. Then also it will be made manifest by what just judgment of God it is that so many — nearly all — of the just judgments of God are now hidden from the senses and minds of mortals; though the faith of the devout is not ignorant that what is hidden is just. — So the most illumined Augustine.
